posts.cooked:
Hi,

Is there a Shopify-compatible app that allows my customers to sign up for re-stock notifications, and allows us to send out re-stock email notifications to my customers, but only based on available inventory? I.E. if I add 8 items back to stock then the first 8 customers on the notify list get emails?

This is a more detailed one. But i have used Back In Stock alert, notify me app. This adds a notify me button on the pdp so users add their email to sign up. Once you restock or add inventory an email automatically gets send.

I.E. if I add 8 items back to stock then the first 8 customers on the notify list get emails? I cannot confirm of this specific behaviour. You can reach out to chat support. Support is great.

Blasting your entire subscriber waiting list when only a small batch arrives is one of the quickest ways to create customer support tickets. When 50 people get an alert for 8 units, 42 shoppers click through to an immediately sold-out page.

To solve this, you need inventory-proportional batching rather than an all-at-once broadcast trigger.

Here is how to configure the pacing logic:

1. Inventory-to-Notification Ratio (1:1 or 1:1.5): Set your restock rule to notify only N subscribers where N equals available inventory (or at most 1.5x inventory to account for non-openers). If you add 8 units, only the first 8 or 12 subscribers in queue should receive the alert.

2. Drip Delay Windows: Do not release subsequent batches immediately. Add a 2 to 4 hour cooldown window between notification batches. If the first 8 subscribers do not purchase within 3 hours and units remain in stock, the next batch of subscribers is triggered automatically.

3. Minimum Stock Threshold: Prevent restock alerts entirely on single-unit returns. If a customer returns 1 damaged or canceled item, you do not want an automated alert firing to dozens of eager buyers. Set a minimum threshold of at least 3 to 5 units before restock triggers activate.

4. Auto-Pause on Stockout: Ensure the trigger listener checks real-time Shopify inventory right before dispatching each batch, pausing the queue immediately if stock drops back to zero.

Adflipr:

Blasting your entire subscriber waiting list when only a small batch arrives is one of the quickest ways to create customer support tickets. When 50 people get an alert for 8 units, 42 shoppers click through to an immediately sold-out page.

Absolutely this ^^^^

What I would do is a “first come first serve” sorting. If 8 stock come in, I would send to the first 4 people who signed up. Then wait. Then send some more.

You don’t really need third party apps. Flow and Messaging. Add tag customers. Create customer segments by tag. Email the segment. Remove tag when sent. All automated. You could even create a metaobject or something to house the waitlist.
Apologies for being dumb on this, but is there a how-to that shows how to build this into my store?

Every store is different, and I’m sure there are some threads here around this kind of thing. I personally like to figure it out myself. Watch these videos to get a brief understanding of what Flow can do.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=edym2_mCj2I

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DAoxfhgaFOU

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SKrzJvb3yCg

Here is one if you use Klavio

one thing to check before building anything: a lot of notify-me apps email the whole list automatically the moment inventory goes above zero. so if you add the 8 back the normal way, everyone gets emailed before any first-8 logic can happen. turn that auto-send off before you restock.

after that, the no-build version works fine for small batches. if your app lets you export the waitlist with signup dates, email the first 8 to 10 yourself, then the next few a couple hours later if anything’s left. the email doesn’t hold the item for them though, so anyone browsing can still buy those 8 first, and one person can take 3. if your theme or an app can cap restocks at 1 per order, i’d add that too.
Check the restock app’s settings for a cap on emails per restock before you pick one, because a lot of them just email the whole list at once and you end up with more people than stock.

Flow can spot the restock, but it can’t email your customers. The inventory quantity changed trigger gives you the variant and the quantity before the change, and the email action in Flow is for internal recipients, so staff get the message, not buyers. There’s no native waitlist either.

The list itself lives in whichever notify-me tool you’re using, so the cap of eight has to come from there. Check whether it has a per-restock email limit or batching setting before you look at anything custom.

If it doesn’t, export the list with signup dates and send to the oldest entries in batches yourself. If the tool writes signups as customer tags or segments, a marketing automation can handle the send instead.

One thing to keep in mind: an email doesn’t reserve stock, so if people are slow to open it you can still oversell.

Hi XpressCS — full disclosure up front, I’m the founder of Nesvo, a Shopify app, and back-in-stock alerts are one of the things it does. It works the way you’re describing.

When a variant sells out, a “Notify me” form appears where the Add to cart button would be, and shoppers leave their email. When stock comes back, Nesvo only emails as many people as there are units, in the order they signed up. So if 8 come back, the first 8 people hear about it.

Not everyone who gets an alert buys, so after 24 hours (you can change that) it checks your stock again and alerts the next people in line if anything’s left. It also checks stock right before every email, so nobody’s told about something that’s already sold out again.

If you want to fine-tune it, you can alert more than one person per unit, hold alerts until a minimum number of units is back, let your best customers hear first, or send one reminder to people who didn’t click.

It isn’t free: back-in-stock comes with the paid plans, which start at $19 a month. The free plan covers profit analytics only.

And if there’s something you need that it doesn’t do yet, tell me. We’re always open to adding features and making changes around what merchants actually need.

You can get part of the way with Flow, but not an exact “8 units, 8 emails” match out of the box. The setup: have signups tag the customer with something like waitlist-SKU123, and trigger on inventory quantity changes when the variant goes from 0 to above 0. A “Get customer data” step can then pull customers with that tag, oldest first, and a loop can add a notify-now tag and remove the waitlist one, so your email tool only sends to that batch. The catch is that the maximum number of results in that step is a fixed setting (up to 100), not the restocked quantity. So you’d pick a batch size that fits your usual restocks and let the rest stay on the waitlist for the next run. If you need it to match the exact quantity every time, that’s where a dedicated back-in-stock app is probably worth it.

ai_summary.summarized_text:
The merchant wants back-in-stock alerts to follow available inventory—for example, notifying only the first eight people when eight units return—rather than emailing the entire waitlist. Participants warn that broad alerts can send more shoppers to a sold-out product than there are units.

Suggested options include checking whether a notify-me app supports per-restock limits or queue batching; manually exporting subscribers by signup date and emailing them in small batches; or using customer tags and marketing automation. Shopify Flow can help identify inventory changes, but it has no native waitlist and its customer lookup has a fixed result limit, so it cannot match each batch exactly to the restocked quantity. Flow’s email action is for staff, not customers. Emails also do not reserve stock, so alerted shoppers may still miss out.

A Shopify app founder said Nesvo automatically notifies subscribers in signup order up to the available quantity, checks stock before sending, and releases another batch after 24 hours if stock remains; paid plans start at $19/month. The thread offers practical paths but no independently verified comparison or final choice.
